description: Binary heaps + priority queues decomposed. Array-backed complete binary tree with the heap property. Sift-up + sift-down maintain the property after insert/extract. Build-heap in O(n) via bottom-up. Variants: d-ary heaps for different fan-out, pairing heaps + Fibonacci heaps for better amortised decrease-key.

sub_mechanisms.name: heap_property
sub_mechanisms.definition: For each node: parent's key ≤ both children's keys (min-heap) or ≥ (max-heap). No constraint between siblings.
sub_mechanisms.why: Weaker than BST property → easier to maintain. Sufficient for extract-min in O(log n): root is always the minimum. The relaxed property is what makes heap operations cheap.

sub_mechanisms.name: array_layout
sub_mechanisms.definition: Complete binary tree stored in array: parent of i is i/2; children of i are 2i and 2i+1 (1-indexed). Or 0-indexed with (i-1)/2, 2i+1, 2i+2.
sub_mechanisms.why: No pointer overhead. Cache-friendly: parent + children near each other in memory. The completeness invariant (tree filled left to right) is what makes this layout work.

sub_mechanisms.name: sift_up
sub_mechanisms.definition: Insert: append to end of array. Sift-up: if new element < parent, swap; repeat until heap property restored.
sub_mechanisms.why: O(log n) work: walking up the tree's height. Single pass; no complex case analysis. The price of insert.

sub_mechanisms.name: sift_down
sub_mechanisms.definition: Extract-min: replace root with last element. Sift-down: if root > smallest child, swap; repeat until heap property restored.
sub_mechanisms.why: O(log n) work walking down. Always swap with the smaller child to maintain order. Combined with deletion of last element, gives O(log n) extract-min.

sub_mechanisms.name: build_heap_bottom_up
sub_mechanisms.definition: Build heap from arbitrary array: start at n/2 (last internal node), sift-down each in reverse order. O(n).
sub_mechanisms.why: Naively, n inserts × O(log n) = O(n log n). Bottom-up exploits that most nodes are near leaves (cheap sift-down). The sum is bounded by 2n via geometric series. Surprising O(n) result.

sub_mechanisms.name: heapsort_use
sub_mechanisms.definition: Sort array via heap: build-heap (O(n)), then extract-max n times (O(n log n)).
sub_mechanisms.why: In-place: array is reused. O(n log n) guaranteed worst case. Lost popularity to quicksort + introsort because of cache behaviour, but used as fallback in introsort.

sub_mechanisms.name: d_ary_heap
sub_mechanisms.definition: Generalisation: each node has d children instead of 2. Sift-up is O(log_d n); sift-down is O(d · log_d n).
sub_mechanisms.why: Higher d: shallower tree, faster decrease-key (sift-up). Lower d: faster extract-min. Dijkstra with d-ary heap can pick d to match graph density.

sub_mechanisms.name: fibonacci_heap
sub_mechanisms.definition: Lazy heap with O(1) amortised insert + decrease-key, O(log n) amortised extract-min. Complex pointer structure of trees.
sub_mechanisms.why: Theoretically optimal for Dijkstra/Prim: with decrease-key in O(1), Dijkstra is O(E + V log V). In practice, constants are large; rarely faster than binary heap. Important theoretical result; less common implementation.

sub_mechanisms.name: pairing_heap
sub_mechanisms.definition: Self-adjusting heap. Insert: pairwise merge with root. Extract-min: combine subtrees pairwise then sequentially.
sub_mechanisms.why: Simpler than Fibonacci. Empirically close to Fibonacci performance with much simpler code. Often the practical choice when Dijkstra performance matters.

sub_mechanisms.name: heap_decrease_key
sub_mechanisms.definition: Lower a key's value: in binary heap, walk up sifting (O(log n)). In Fibonacci: cut the node + cascading-cut (O(1) amortised).
sub_mechanisms.why: Critical operation for Dijkstra + Prim: relax an edge decreases the dest's key. Frequency of decrease-key vs extract-min determines best heap variant.

sub_mechanisms.name: priority_queue_abstraction
sub_mechanisms.definition: Interface: insert(item, priority), extract-best, peek. Implementation is a heap underneath.
sub_mechanisms.why: Many algorithms (Dijkstra, A*, scheduling) need 'next best thing to do' semantics. Decoupling the abstraction from implementation lets the heap variant be swapped per workload.

derivation_rules.name: heap_property_sufficient_for_extract_min
then: the root is the minimum element
derivation_rules.why: Each node ≤ both children → recursively root ≤ everything. Direct from the invariant. Lets extract-min be O(1) lookup + O(log n) restoration.

derivation_rules.name: build_heap_O_n_via_amortised_cost
then: total work is O(n) not O(n log n)
derivation_rules.why: Most nodes are near the leaves (cheap sift-down: O(1) or O(2)). Few nodes are near the root (expensive: O(log n)). The sum ∑ h × n/2^(h+1) is bounded by 2n. The classical surprising O(n) result.

derivation_rules.name: array_layout_cache_friendly
derivation_rules.why: Parent + children in array indices i, 2i, 2i+1 are close in memory. Modern CPUs prefetch sequentially. Array-backed heap beats pointer-based heap by an order of magnitude in practice, even though both are O(log n).

derivation_rules.name: fibonacci_heap_optimal_for_dijkstra_theoretical
if: Dijkstra is implemented with Fibonacci heap
then: total time is O(E + V log V)
derivation_rules.why: Each decrease-key is O(1) amortised; n total. Each extract-min is O(log V); V total. Better than binary heap's O((E + V) log V). In practice, binary heap usually wins on real graphs due to constants.

derivation_rules.name: d_ary_heap_optimises_for_workload
derivation_rules.why: Sift-up cost scales with log_d (shallower tree). Sift-down cost scales with d × log_d (more children to scan). Pick d based on operation mix: dense graphs (many edges per vertex) favour higher d.
